drills.q: In 8-bit two's complement, what value does the bit pattern 10000000 represent?
options: It is a trap representation
drills.why: The top bit carries a weight of -128 rather than flagging a sign. There is no negative zero in two's complement, which is one of the three reasons it won.

drills.q: Why did two's complement beat sign-magnitude for integers?
options: It represents a wider range of values for the same bit count
One zero, and addition that works on signed and unsigned alike, so the
It makes multiplication cheaper in hardware
It was the first scheme anyone tried
drills.why: Sign-magnitude has two zeroes and needs a separate signed adder. Two's complement makes subtraction into addition with one operand inverted and the carry in set, which is one control bit rather than a second circuit.

options: There is one more negative value than positive, so its negation is out of
Negation is undefined for all values in C
The sign bit cannot be cleared without losing the value
It has an answer, but only on two's complement machines
drills.why: 32 bits give 2147483648 negative values and 2147483647 positive ones. The asymmetry is the price of having exactly one zero, and it is why abs(INT_MIN) is negative everywhere.

drills.q: What does "undefined behaviour" state about a program?
options: The result is unpredictable and may vary between runs
The compiler will produce a diagnostic
The program broke a precondition the standard requires it to satisfy, so
The behaviour depends on the target processor
drills.why: It is a precondition, not a warning about variability. Once it is violated, the standard says nothing at all about what the implementation must do, which is why two compilers can produce different answers and both be right.

drills.q: The same signed-overflow program compiled by gcc and by clang at -O2 prints different values. What follows?
options: One of the compilers has a bug worth reporting
Nothing is wrong. There is no correct answer for either to produce
The program depends on the processor rather than the compiler
The difference would disappear at -O0
drills.why: Measured: gcc emits mov esi, 1 and clang emits xor esi, esi for the identical source. Both constant-folded the comparison, using different reasoning, and neither is obliged to agree with the other.

drills.q: Why does an unsigned loop counter often produce worse code than a signed one?
options: Unsigned arithmetic uses more instructions on x86-64
Unsigned wraparound is defined, so the compiler must preserve it and
Signed values fit in registers more efficiently
The optimiser has more passes written for signed types
drills.why: Because signed overflow is undefined, the compiler may promote the counter to 64 bits, strength-reduce the address arithmetic to a walking pointer and unroll. With an unsigned counter it must keep recomputing the index, because the wrap is a behaviour the program is entitled to.

drills.q: int a = -1; unsigned b = 1; What does a < b evaluate to, and why?
options: 1, because -1 is less than 1
0, because a converts to unsigned first and becomes 4294967295
It is undefined behaviour
It depends on the optimisation level
drills.why: The usual arithmetic conversions turn the signed operand unsigned when both have the same rank. The comparison is well defined and it does not mean what it appears to say. -Wsign-compare, from -Wextra, names it.

drills.q: Why does for (size_t i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--) never terminate?
options: n - 1 overflows when n is zero
i >= 0 is always true for an unsigned type, and decrementing 0 wraps to
The compiler removes the condition as undefined behaviour
It terminates, but only after 2^64 iterations
drills.why: An unsigned value has no negative range for the test to detect. Loop from n down to 1 and index with i - 1, which keeps the index type matching the container's.

drills.q: Running with -fsanitize=undefined but without -fno-sanitize-recover=all, a program overflows. What happens?
options: The program aborts immediately
The sanitizer prints a runtime error and the program continues and exits 0
Nothing, because the sanitizer only checks memory
The compiler refuses to build it
drills.why: Measured: the diagnostic appears on stderr and the exit status is still 0, so a test suite reports a pass over a program that has already broken its contract. The recover flag is not optional in a checking harness.

drills.q: Which overflow test is well defined?
options: if (a + b < 0)
if (b > 0 && a > INT_MAX - b)
if ((long)(a + b) > INT_MAX)
if (a + b < a)
drills.why: The others all perform the addition first and then examine a value the standard says does not exist, so the compiler may conclude the test is never true and delete it. Checking the operands asks a question the standard answers.

options: The sum, or zero if it overflowed
True when the operation overflowed, having written the wrapped result to
True when the operation succeeded
An error code matching errno
drills.why: It reports the overflow rather than the success, which is the opposite of what most people guess and the reason a wrapper usually negates it. C23 standardises the same family as ckd_add.

drills.q: Why is mov eax, eax not a no-op on x86-64?
options: Writing a 32-bit register zeroes the upper 32 bits of the 64-bit register
It flushes the instruction pipeline
It is a no-op, and assemblers remove it
It sign-extends the value into the full register
drills.why: Writes to 32-bit registers zero-extend; writes to 16-bit and 8-bit ones do not. AMD chose that when extending the architecture because it breaks the dependency on the register's previous value, which lets the renamer avoid serialising.

drills.q: Reading one byte through a char* on a target where char is signed, what does the byte 0xFF become as an int?
options: -1, because the value sign-extends
Implementation-defined and unusable
0xFF, unchanged, since no conversion happens
drills.why: Plain char is signed here, so the compiler emits movsx and copies the top bit into the new high bits. Reading through unsigned char* emits movzx instead. This is why char is the wrong type for a byte of data.

drills.q: mid(2, -1) gives 0 for (a + b) / 2 and 1 for a + (b - a) / 2. Why?
options: The second form overflows
Integer division truncates toward zero, so (-3) / 2 is -1 rather than -2
The first form has undefined behaviour for negative operands
They are the same function and the difference is a rounding mode
drills.why: No overflow is involved at these values. The two expressions are genuinely different functions on negative inputs, and the overflow-safe form is not simply a more careful way of writing the same thing.

drills.q: You want the compiler to treat signed overflow as two's complement wraparound. What do you give up?
options: Nothing, it is purely a safety improvement
The loop optimisations that depend on assuming a signed counter only
Portability, since the flag changes the meaning of the standard
Nothing at compile time, but the program runs slower on every operation
drills.why: -fwrapv defines the behaviour, and defining it is exactly what stops the compiler from promoting induction variables, strength-reducing addresses and unrolling. The flag is a real trade, not a free check.
